content.title: About
content.content: Brandy is a distilled spirit made by double‑distilling fermented grape wine. It boasts a rich aroma, deep flavor, and a characteristic golden‑amber hue. Many brandies are aged in oak barrels, which impart notes of vanilla, caramel, and spice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “brandy” comes from the Dutch “brandewijn,” meaning “burnt wine.”
The most famous type of brandy is Cognac, produced in a strictly defined region of France.
Traditionally, brandy is served in small snifters that allow its aromas to fully develop.
In some cuisines, brandy is used for flambéing desserts and sauces.
Aging in oak can last from a few years to several decades, influencing taste and price.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Polyphenols and other compounds in brandy may help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: A modest amount of brandy after a meal is traditionally believed to support digestion.

items.title: Improves circulation
items.content: Ethanol in small doses can dilate blood vessels, enhancing blood flow.

items.title: Alcohol dependence
items.content: Excessive consumption of brandy can lead to addiction and liver damage.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Alcohol may amplify the effects of certain medications, including sedatives and anticoagulants.

items.title: Pregnancy and lactation
items.content: Alcohol intake is contraindicated during pregnancy and while breastfeeding.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Brandy is typically served in small glasses at room temperature. It can be enjoyed neat, on the rocks, or in cocktails. For a fragrant experience, let the spirit breathe in the glass for a few minutes before sipping.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep brandy in a tightly sealed bottle, away from direct sunlight and temperature fluctuations. After opening, store the bottle in a cool place, but not in the refrigerator, to preserve its aroma.
